sections: Geography & landmarks
Regions
The Midlands, East Anglia, the West Country, the North of England and the South East are geographical/cultural areas, not constituent countries.
Rivers
The Thames flows through London; the Severn is the longest river in the UK.
Relief
The Pennines are often called the backbone of England; Scafell Pike is England’s highest mountain.
Sites
Stonehenge (prehistoric monument), Hadrian’s Wall (Roman frontier), Canterbury Cathedral (medieval pilgrimage).
History & institutions
The Norman Conquest followed William of Normandy’s victory at the Battle of Hastings.
Magna Carta was sealed by King John at Runnymede; its later constitutional importance is greater than its immediate effects.
The Act of Supremacy recognised Henry VIII as Supreme Head of the Church of England.
England was a republic/Commonwealth and then Protectorate before the Restoration of the monarchy.
The Acts of Union united the kingdoms of England (including Wales) and Scotland as Great Britain.
Culture & symbols
Patron saint
St George; St George’s Day is 23 April.
Flag
St George’s Cross: a red cross on white.
Emblem
The Tudor rose combines the red rose of Lancaster and the white rose of York.
Literature
Geoffrey Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales; William Shakespeare is associated with Stratford-upon-Avon and the Globe Theatre.

challenge.q: Which 1215 document is associated with King John and Runnymede?
challenge.why: Magna Carta was sealed in 1215; the Bill of Rights dates to 1689.

sections: Geography & landmarks
Regions
Highlands and Lowlands are broad geographical divisions; the Hebrides, Orkney and Shetland are major island groups.
Peaks
Ben Nevis is the highest mountain in the UK.
Water
Loch Ness is famous for its legend; Loch Lomond is a major freshwater loch.
Cities
Edinburgh is the capital; Glasgow is Scotland’s largest city.
History & institutions
Robert the Bruce defeated English forces at the Battle of Bannockburn.
James VI of Scotland became James I of England, creating a union of crowns, not yet a single state.
The Acts of Union created the Kingdom of Great Britain.
The devolved Scottish Parliament opened following the 1997 referendum and the Scotland Act 1998.
Culture & symbols
Patron saint
St Andrew; St Andrew’s Day is 30 November.
Flag
The Saltire: a white diagonal cross on blue.
Emblem
The thistle; the unicorn is Scotland’s heraldic animal.
Literature
Robert Burns wrote Auld Lang Syne; Sir Walter Scott wrote historical novels including Ivanhoe.

options: The Acts of Union were passed
James VI of Scotland inherited the English throne
The Battle of Bannockburn took place
challenge.why: 1603 was the Union of the Crowns; political union followed in 1707.

sections: Geography & landmarks
Relief
Eryri (Snowdonia) is a mountainous region; Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) is Wales’s highest mountain.
Parks
Eryri, Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons) and Pembrokeshire Coast are national parks.
Cities
Cardiff is the capital; Swansea and Newport are other major cities.
Castles
Caernarfon, Conwy, Beaumaris and Harlech castles are part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
History & institutions
Edward I conquered the principality ruled by Llywelyn ap Gruffudd; English rule expanded.
The Laws in Wales Acts integrated Wales more fully into the English legal and administrative system.
The National Assembly for Wales first met; the institution is now called the Senedd (Welsh Parliament).
Culture & symbols
Patron saint
St David; St David’s Day is 1 March.
Flag
A red dragon on a white-and-green field; the dragon is not represented separately on the Union Flag.
Emblems
The daffodil and the leek.
Language
Welsh (Cymraeg) and English are official languages in Wales.
Tradition
The Eisteddfod is a festival and competition of literature, music and performance.

challenge.q: Which symbol appears on the Welsh national flag?
challenge.why: The red dragon is central to the flag of Wales.

sections: Geography & landmarks
Geography
Northern Ireland occupies the north-east of the island of Ireland; the Republic of Ireland is a separate state.
Water
Lough Neagh is the largest freshwater lake by area in the British Isles.
Coast
The Giant’s Causeway in County Antrim is a UNESCO World Heritage Site with basalt columns.
Cities
Belfast is the capital; Derry/Londonderry is another major city.
History & institutions
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland was formed.
Partition left six north-eastern counties within the UK; the Irish Free State emerged in 1922.
The Belfast/Good Friday Agreement provided a framework for power-sharing and the peace process.
Devolution
The Northern Ireland Assembly meets at Parliament Buildings, Stormont.
Culture & symbols
Patron saint
St Patrick is strongly associated with Ireland as a whole; St Patrick’s Day is 17 March.
Symbols
The flax flower and shamrock are cultural symbols; their use and political associations vary.
Flag distinction
Northern Ireland has no single officially adopted regional flag for general use. The former Ulster Banner is historical and politically sensitive.
Literature
C. S. Lewis was born in Belfast; Seamus Heaney was born in County Londonderry.

challenge.q: Which agreement is associated with the 1998 peace process?
challenge.why: The Belfast/Good Friday Agreement was reached in 1998.
